newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel to tell Albright-no Scientology persecution.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel to tell Albright-no Scientology persecution.

text.p: Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel will tell U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright next week that members of the Church of Scientology are not persecuted in Germany.
"There can be no question of persecution of Scientology in this country," Kinkel told the Berliner Kurier newspaper in an interview published on Friday.
Kinkel will meet Albright when she visits Germany on Sunday and Monday as part of her first overseas trip since taking office last month.
The U.S.-based organisation says it is a bona fide religion. It accuses Germany of hounding its members, and compares Bonn's stance to Nazi persecution of the Jews before World War Two.
The U.S. State Department's annual survey of human rights problems listed Scientologists' allegations, and a senior department official said the survey was an expression of "serious concern".
But Kinkel said he would tell Albright that Scientology was neither a religion nor a philosophy of life, but an organisation with unequivocally economic aims.

Germany does not accord Scientology the status of a religion, believing it exploits its members to make profits from expensive self-improvement courses. Several leading officials have said it might be a threat to democracy.

Kinkel said differences between the U.S. and German views on the group were the result of the two countries' different histories and constitutions. "Our history teaches us to be particularly on our guard," Kinkel said.
"Given Scientology's practices, which are also not uncontroversial in the United States, the protection of our citizens takes priority," he said.
Kinkel said he and Albright agreed that Scientology's use of the Holocaust as a comparison was a falsification of history, and insulted victims of the Nazi period.
Scientology is a religious philosophy founded in 1954 by U.S. science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard.

The southern state of Bavaria has been at the forefront of measures to combat the group, excluding companies run by Scientologists from public tenders and asking applicants for public sector jobs whether they belong to the organisation.
Bavaria has also placed Scientology under observation by its anti-extremist watchdog.
